title: Antisemitism today
hookLine: old hatreds return, and communities answer with resilience

lines: A WOODEN DOOR ON YOM KIPPUR.
cards: On Yom Kippur, in the German city of Halle, a small congregation is praying through the long fast behind a heavy wooden door. Outside, a gunman tries to force his way in. He shoots at the door, again and again.
The door holds. Unable to get in, he turns on people in the street nearby. And behind the door, the congregation keeps praying.

teach.h: AN OLD HATRED IN NEW COSTUMES.
teach.b: Antisemitism is hatred of Jews for being Jews.
It is old, and it keeps changing costumes: religious blame, racial theories, conspiracy stories about secret power or money, and sometimes anger at Israel that slides into blaming any Jew anywhere.

In recent years it has come back in forms people had hoped were finished: attacks on synagogues in Pittsburgh and in Halle, graffiti on gravestones, harassment online and on the street, families wondering whether to wear a kippah or a Star of David in public.
The Passover Haggadah has a line for this.

It says that in every generation there are those who rise up to destroy the Jewish people, and that the Holy One saves them. Around the Seder table it's sung with cups raised, and then the meal goes on.
The answer today looks like that.
After the Pittsburgh attack, neighbors of many faiths came to stand in synagogues the next Shabbat, and Muslim groups raised money for the victims' families.
Guards now stand outside some synagogues, and the services still happen. Children still go to Hebrew school.

teach.h: BE STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.
teach.b: God's words to Joshua, before he leads the people across the Jordan, are a short command: "Be strong and of good courage." The verse goes on: don't be afraid or dismayed, for God is with you wherever you go.
It's said at the riverbank, before the crossing, not after.
This week walked from secret kitchens in Moscow to a zigzag on a bridge, from Heschel's praying legs to a Mississippi summer, from peace treaties to an argument at a Shabbat table.
Each story had a hard thing in it, and someone who didn't step back.

how: At the Passover Seder, Jews sing that in every generation enemies rise up and God saves them, and today some synagogues keep holding services with security at the door and neighbors of other faiths invited in.

games.q: it's the week after an attack on a synagogue. a community must decide what to do this Shabbat. what does it do?
o: cancel services until things feel safe.
hold services, with guards outside and neighbors invited in.
games.why: in the stories told today, communities kept their doors open, with guards outside, and neighbors of other faiths came to stand with them.

practice: Bring to mind a Jewish friend, coworker or neighbor, or if none comes to mind, a synagogue or Jewish school near you and the people who walk through its doors, and hold them for a moment, by name if you can.

Think of one simple message you could send, just thinking of you, presence rather than a speech; if you're Jewish yourself, you can let someone check on you, or reach out to someone else. If you pray, hold them in prayer.
